summary.text: For \(p\ge7\), finite-field power-sum vanishing together with reciprocal reflection and binomial-transform identities gives, modulo \(p^5\), \(d^2=0\) and the two constituent sums as \(3(1-3d)\) and \(3+12d\), where \(d=p^2\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}k^{-2}\). Their prescribed powers cancel the linear \(d\)-terms and hence give \(3^7\); the exceptional primes \(3\) and \(5\) are handled by direct finite evaluation.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 S_1(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{2n}\binom{n+k-1}{k},\qquad
 S_2(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{2n}\binom{n+k-1}{k}^2.
\]
Then
\[
 a(n)=S_1(n)^4S_2(n)^3.
\]
We prove that, for every prime \(p\geq 3\),
\[
 a(p)\equiv a(1)\pmod {p^5}.
\]
Since \(S_1(1)=S_2(1)=3\), we have
\[
 a(1)=3^4 3^3=3^7=2187.
\]
Thus it suffices to prove \(a(p)\equiv2187\pmod {p^5}\).

We first treat primes \(p\geq7\). All the calculations in this part take place in the commutative ring
\[
 R=\mathbb Z/p^5\mathbb Z.
\]
Write \(t\) for the class of \(p\) in \(R\), put \(N=p-1\), and, for \(0\leq i<N\), put
\[
 u_i=(i+1)^{-1}\in R.
\]
These inverses exist because \(1\leq i+1<p\), hence \(i+1\) is relatively prime to \(p^5\). In particular,
\[
 (i+1)u_i=1.
\]
For integers \(r\geq1\) and \(0\leq m\leq N\), define the truncated harmonic sums
\[
 P_r(m)=\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}u_i^r,
\]
and abbreviate \(P_r=P_r(N)\). We shall also need
\[
 D_{a,b}=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}P_a(j)u_j^b,
 \qquad
 Q=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}P_1(j)^2u_j^2.
\]

We will establish enough harmonic congruences to evaluate both \(S_1(p)\) and \(S_2(p)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Two finite-sum transforms
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For a function \(f\) on the positive integers, define
\[
 T_m(f)=\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}(-1)^i\binom m{i+1}f(i+1).
\]
Also, for a function \(g\), define its weighted partial-sum transform
\[
 (Hg)(m)=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}u_jg(j+1).
\]
The basic alternating-binomial tail identity is
\[
 \sum_{i=j}^{m-1}(-1)^i\binom m{i+1}
   =(-1)^j\binom{m-1}{j}.                                      \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, Pascal's identity writes the summand as
\[
 (-1)^i\binom{m-1}{i}-(-1)^{i+1}\binom{m-1}{i+1},
\]
so the sum telescopes.

Another elementary identity, using \((i+1)u_i=(j+1)u_j=1\), is
\[
 u_i\binom{i+1}{j+1}=u_j\binom ij.                              \tag{2}
\]
It follows from
\[
 (i+1)\binom ij=(j+1)\binom{i+1}{j+1}.
\]

Changing the order in the triangular double sums and using (1) and (2) gives two transform identities:
\[
 T_m(Hf)=u_{m-1}T_m(f),                                         \tag{3}
\]
and
\[
 \sum_{i=0}^{m-1}u_iT_{i+1}(f)
 =T_m\bigl(k\mapsto u_{k-1}f(k)\bigr).                         \tag{4}
\]
For completeness, in (3) the coefficient of \(f(j+1)\) after reversing the sums is
\[
 u_j\sum_{i=j}^{m-1}(-1)^i\binom m{i+1}
 =u_j(-1)^j\binom{m-1}{j}
 =u_{m-1}(-1)^j\binom m{j+1},
\]
which proves (3). For (4), the coefficient produced by reversing the sums is evaluated with (2) and the hockey-stick identity
\[
 \sum_{i=j}^{m-1}\binom ij=\binom m{j+1}.
\]

Taking \(f=1\) in (1) gives \(T_m(1)=1\). Equations (3) and (4) then imply
\[
 T_m(k\mapsto u_{k-1})=P_1(m).                                 \tag{5}
\]
Using (4) once more and the elementary identity
\[
 2\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}u_iP_1(i+1)=P_1(m)^2+P_2(m),
\]
we obtain
\[
 2T_m(k\mapsto u_{k-1}^2)=P_1(m)^2+P_2(m).                    \tag{6}
\]
The displayed elementary identity follows by induction from
\(P_r(m+1)=P_r(m)+u_m^r\), or simply by expanding the square of \(P_1(m)\).

A fourth-weight version of the same duality will also be needed. Since
\[
 P_3(m)=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}u_j\,u_j^2=H(k\mapsto u_{k-1}^2)(m),
\]
(3), (4), and (6) give
\[
 2T_m\bigl(k\mapsto u_{k-1}P_3(k)\bigr)
 =\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}u_i^2\bigl(P_1(i+1)^2+P_2(i+1)\bigr).        \tag{7}
\]
Expanding the right side and using
\(P_r(i+1)=P_r(i)+u_i^r\) yields
\[
 \sum_{i=0}^{m-1}u_i^2\bigl(P_1(i+1)^2+P_2(i+1)\bigr)
 =Q(m)+2D_{1,3}(m)+D_{2,2}(m)+2P_4(m),                         \tag{8}
\]
where the notation on the right is truncated at \(m\).

We shall also repeatedly use the product relation
\[
 P_a(m)P_b(m)=D_{a,b}(m)+D_{b,a}(m)+P_{a+b}(m).                \tag{9}
\]
This follows by partitioning all ordered pairs of indices according as the first is smaller than, larger than, or equal to the second.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Vanishing identities modulo \(p\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Reduce the \(u_i\)'s modulo \(p\). They become the inverses of \(1,2,\ldots,p-1\) in \(\mathbb F_p\). For \(1\leq r<p-1\),
\[
 P_r=0\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_p.                              \tag{10}
\]
Indeed, inversion permutes \(\mathbb F_p^\times\), so \(P_r\) is the sum of the \(r\)-th powers of all nonzero elements. That sum is zero when \(p-1\nmid r\): multiplying the sum by the \(r\)-th power of an element whose \(r\)-th power is not \(1\) leaves the same sum and forces it to vanish. Thus, because \(p\geq7\),
\[
 P_1=P_2=P_3=P_4=0\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_p.                 \tag{11}
\]

Reflection of the nonzero residues gives
\[
 u_{N-1-i}=-u_i\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_p.                    \tag{12}
\]
It follows that
\[
 P_1(N-j)=P_1(N)+P_1(j)=P_1(j),                                \tag{13}
\]
where the last equality uses \(P_1(N)=0\). Reflecting the sum defining \(D_{1,3}\), and using (12), (13), and
\(P_1(j+1)=P_1(j)+u_j\), gives
\[
 D_{1,3}=-D_{1,3}-P_4.
\]
Since \(P_4=0\) and \(2\neq0\) in \(\mathbb F_p\),
\[
 D_{1,3}=0.                                                     \tag{14}
\]
By (9), applied first with \((a,b)=(2,2)\) and then with \((1,3)\), equations (11) and (14) give
\[
 D_{2,2}=0,
 \qquad D_{3,1}=0.                                             \tag{15}
\]

It remains to show \(Q=0\) modulo \(p\). In \(\mathbb F_p\),
\[
 \binom{p-1}{k}=(-1)^k\qquad(0\leq k<p),
\]
so
\[
 T_N(f)=-\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}f(i+1).                              \tag{16}
\]
Apply (7) with \(m=N\). By (16), its left side is
\[
 -2\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}u_iP_3(i+1).
\]
But
\[
 \sum_{i=0}^{N-1}u_iP_3(i+1)=D_{3,1}+P_4=0
\]
by (11) and (15). Hence (7) and (8), together with (11), (14), and (15), imply
\[
 Q=0\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_p.                               \tag{17}
\]

If an element of \(R=\mathbb Z/p^5\mathbb Z\) reduces to zero modulo \(p\), it is a multiple of \(t=p\), and therefore multiplication by \(t^4\) kills it. Lifting (11), (14), (15), and (17) to \(R\), we consequently have
\[
\begin{aligned}
&t^4P_1=t^4P_2=t^4P_4=0,\\
&t^4D_{1,3}=t^4D_{2,2}=t^4Q=0.                                \tag{18}
\end{aligned}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Stronger harmonic relations modulo \(p^5\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

The reflection relation can be refined in \(R\). Pair \(u_i=(i+1)^{-1}\) with
\(u_{N-1-i}=(p-(i+1))^{-1}\). Since \(t^5=0\), the finite geometric expansion gives
\[
 t u_{N-1-i}
 =-tu_i-t^2u_i^2-t^3u_i^3-t^4u_i^4,                           \tag{19}
\]
and cubing the same relation gives
\[
 t^3u_{N-1-i}^3=-t^3u_i^3-3t^4u_i^4.                         \tag{20}
\]
For instance, (19) is obtained by solving
\((t-(i+1))u_{N-1-i}=1\) with the geometric series through degree four; all omitted terms contain \(t^5\).

Sum (20) over \(i\), using reflection of the index set. We find
\[
 t^3P_3=-t^3P_3-3t^4P_4.
\]
By (18), the last term vanishes. Because \(p\geq7\), \(2\) is invertible in \(R\), and hence
\[
 t^3P_3=0.                                                     \tag{21}
\]
Similarly, summing (19) gives
\[
 tP_1=-tP_1-t^2P_2-t^3P_3-t^4P_4.
\]
Using (18) and (21),
\[
 2tP_1=-t^2P_2.                                                \tag{22}
\]
Squaring (22), and using \(t^4P_2=0\), yields
\(4t^2P_1^2=0\). Since \(4\) is invertible in \(R\),
\[
 t^2P_1^2=0.                                                   \tag{23}
\]

One additional weighted relation is required:
\[
 2t^3D_{1,2}=3t^2P_2.                                         \tag{24}
\]
We now derive it.

For \(0\leq i<N\), the elementary product formula for a binomial coefficient gives
\[
 \binom{p-1}{i+1}
 =(-1)^{i+1}\prod_{j=0}^{i}(1-tu_j).                          \tag{25}
\]
Expanding the product through degree two after multiplying by \(2t^2\) gives
\[
 2t^2\prod_{j=0}^{i}(1-tu_j)
 =2t^2-2t^3P_1(i+1)
   +t^4\bigl(P_1(i+1)^2-P_2(i+1)\bigr).                       \tag{26}
\]
All higher terms vanish because they contain \(t^5\). Multiplying (25) by the signs in \(T_N\), then summing against \(u_i^2\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
2t^2T_N(k\mapsto u_{k-1}^2)
={}&-2t^2P_2+2t^3(D_{1,2}+P_3)\\
&-t^4\bigl(Q+2D_{1,3}-D_{2,2}\bigr).                         \tag{27}
\end{aligned}
\]
Here one uses
\[
 \sum_i u_i^2P_1(i+1)=D_{1,2}+P_3
\]
and the direct expansion
\[
 \sum_i u_i^2\bigl(P_1(i+1)^2-P_2(i+1)\bigr)
 =Q+2D_{1,3}-D_{2,2}.
\]
On the other hand, (6), multiplied by \(t^2\), says that the left side of (27) is
\[
 t^2(P_1^2+P_2)=t^2P_2
\]
by (23). Substituting (18) and (21) into (27) now leaves
\[
 t^2P_2=-2t^2P_2+2t^3D_{1,2},
\]
which is exactly (24).

Let
\[
 d=t^2P_2.                                                      \tag{28}
\]
Equation (18) immediately gives
\[
 d^2=t^4P_2^2=P_2(t^4P_2)=0.                                  \tag{29}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Evaluation of the first truncated sum
--------------------------------------------------------------------

The hockey-stick identity gives
\[
 S_1(p)=\sum_{k=0}^{2p}\binom{p+k-1}{k}=\binom{3p}{p}.         \tag{30}
\]
Moreover,
\[
 \binom{3p}{p}
 =3\binom{3p-1}{p-1}
 =3\prod_{i=0}^{N-1}(1+2tu_i).                                \tag{31}
\]

We evaluate the product in (31). For arbitrary \(x_i\), expansion in elementary symmetric functions, expressed in terms of the power sums, gives, whenever \(x^5=0\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
24\prod_i(1+xu_i)={}&24+24xP_1+12x^2(P_1^2-P_2)\\
&+4x^3(P_1^3-3P_1P_2+2P_3)\\
&+x^4(P_1^4-6P_1^2P_2+3P_2^2+8P_1P_3-6P_4).                 \tag{32}
\end{aligned}
\]
This identity can also be checked directly by adjoining one factor at a time and using \(P_r(m+1)=P_r(m)+u_m^r\).

Put \(x=2t\) in (32). Using (18), (21), (22), and (23), every term reduces to give
\[
 24\prod_{i=0}^{N-1}(1+2tu_i)=24(1-3t^2P_2)=24(1-3d).
\]
Since \(p\geq7\), \(24\) is invertible in \(R\). Thus
\[
 \prod_{i=0}^{N-1}(1+2tu_i)=1-3d.
\]
Equations (30) and (31) therefore give
\[
 S_1(p)=3(1-3d)\quad\text{in }R.                              \tag{33}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. A binomial representation and evaluation of the square sum
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We first transform \(S_2(p)\). The following identity is a consequence of Vandermonde's convolution:
\[
 \binom{n+k}{n}^2
 =\sum_{j=0}^{n}\binom nj\binom{n+j}{j}\binom{n+k}{n+j}.       \tag{34}
\]
To see this, write
\[
 \binom{n+k}{n}=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\binom nj\binom kj

after applying Vandermonde and symmetry, multiply by \(\binom{n+k}{n}\), and use
\[
 \binom{n+k}{n}\binom kj
 =\binom{n+k}{n+j}\binom{n+j}{j}.
\]
Summing (34) over \(k=0,\ldots,m\) and applying the hockey-stick identity gives
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{m}\binom{n+k}{n}^2
 =\sum_{j=0}^{n}\binom nj\binom{n+j}{j}
   \binom{n+m+1}{n+j+1}.                                      \tag{35}
\]
Take \(n=p-1\) and \(m=2p\). Since
\(\binom{p+k-1}{k}=\binom{p+k-1}{p-1}\), equation (35) becomes
\[
 S_2(p)=\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}
 \binom{p-1}{j}\binom{p-1+j}{j}\binom{3p}{p+j}.              \tag{36}
\]
The \(j=0\) term is \(B=\binom{3p}{p}\).

We now evaluate the remaining terms. For \(0\leq j<N\), a direct calculation from factorials gives
\[
 (p+j)\binom{p-1+j}{j}\binom{3p}{p+j}
 =p\binom{3p}{p}\binom{2p}{j}.                                \tag{37}
\]
Also, the product formula (25), together with the analogous formula for \(\binom{2p}{j+1}\), yields
\[
 \binom{p-1}{j+1}\binom{2p}{j+1}
 =-2tu_j(1-tu_j)
   \prod_{i=0}^{j-1}(1-tu_i)(1-2tu_i).                         \tag{38}
\]
Combining (37) and (38), and dividing only by units such as \(j+1\) and \(1+tu_j\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\binom{p-1}{j+1}\binom{p+j}{j+1}\binom{3p}{p+j+1}\\
&\quad=-2Bt^2u_j^2(1-2tu_j+2t^2u_j^2)
 \prod_{i=0}^{j-1}(1-tu_i)(1-2tu_i).                          \tag{39}
\end{aligned}
\]
The factor \(1+tu_j\) is invertible because its inverse, modulo \(t^5\), is
\[
 1-tu_j+t^2u_j^2-t^3u_j^3+t^4u_j^4.
\]
This also explains the quadratic factor in (39): after cancellation,
\((1-tu_j)/(1+tu_j)=1-2tu_j+2t^2u_j^2-2t^3u_j^3+2t^4u_j^4\), and terms beyond degree two disappear once multiplied by \(t^2\) and by the remaining factors in the calculation.

It remains to sum (39). First observe the product expansion
\[
\begin{aligned}
2t^2\prod_{i=0}^{j-1}(1-tu_i)(1-2tu_i)
={}&2t^2-6t^3P_1(j)\\
&+t^4\bigl(9P_1(j)^2-5P_2(j)\bigr).                           \tag{40}
\end{aligned}
\]
Indeed, each paired factor is \(1-3tu_i+2t^2u_i^2\), and multiplying these factors through degree two gives (40). Multiplying (40) by
\(1-2tu_j+2t^2u_j^2\), summing (39) over \(j=0,\ldots,N-1\), and collecting the definitions of the weighted sums gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&S_2(p)-B\\
={}&-B\bigl(2t^2P_2-6t^3D_{1,2}-4t^3P_3\\
&\hspace{42mm}+t^4(9Q-5D_{2,2}+12D_{1,3}+4P_4)\bigr).         \tag{41}
\end{aligned}
\]
Now apply (18), (21), and (24). All the terms in the last line of (41) vanish, while
\[
 2t^2P_2-6t^3D_{1,2}
 =2t^2P_2-3(2t^3D_{1,2})
 =2t^2P_2-9t^2P_2=-7t^2P_2.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 S_2(p)=B+7Bd.                                                  \tag{42}
\]
By (33), \(B=3(1-3d)\), and \(d^2=0\). Therefore
\[
 S_2(p)=3(1-3d)+21(1-3d)d=3+12d.                              \tag{43}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Completion for \(p\geq7\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

From (33), (43), and \(d^2=0\),
\[
 a(p)=\bigl(3(1-3d)\bigr)^4(3+12d)^3.
\]
Factor out \(3^7\):
\[
 a(p)=3^7(1-3d)^4(1+4d)^3.
\]
Because \(d^2=0\), the binomial theorem gives
\[
 (1-3d)^4=1-12d,
 \qquad
 (1+4d)^3=1+12d.
\]
Their product is \(1-144d^2=1\). Hence in \(R\),
\[
 a(p)=3^7=2187.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
 a(p)\equiv2187\pmod {p^5}
\]
for every prime \(p\geq7\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. The primes \(3\) and \(5\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

These two primes are checked directly from the defining finite sums.

For \(p=3\),
\[
 S_1(3)=84,
 \qquad
 S_2(3)=1596.
\]
Modulo \(3^5=243\),
\[
 84^4\equiv81,
 \qquad
 1596^3\equiv27,

a(3)\equiv81\cdot27\equiv0\pmod{243}.
\]
Also \(2187=9\cdot243\), so \(a(3)\equiv2187\pmod{3^5}\).

For \(p=5\),
\[
 S_1(5)=3003,
 \qquad
 S_2(5)=1933503.
\]
Modulo \(5^5=3125\), direct exponentiation gives
\[
 3003^4\equiv2206,
 \qquad
 1933503^3\equiv1402,

a(5)\equiv2206\cdot1402\equiv2187\pmod{3125}.
\]

Thus the result holds for \(p=3\), \(p=5\), and every prime \(p\geq7\). Since \(a(1)=2187\), we conclude that for every prime \(p\geq3\),
\[
 \boxed{a(p)\equiv a(1)\pmod {p^5}}.
\]
